    Huron · Implementation atlas

    Inside the Rawstore

    Descriptors, candidates, and one exclusive rename: the classes and primitives that turn uploaded bytes into durable, sealed, verifiable Raw revisions on a single filesystem.

    4 rawstore classesDescriptor-based durability9 UML viewsOffline-ready

    Implementation snapshot: 16 September 2026, working tree based on e71e685. The editable Markdown source contains all Mermaid diagrams and responsibility notes.

    The rawstore is Huron's evidence tier on one POSIX filesystem: it receives upload parts into private staging, materializes each file as an independent verified copy, publishes a finished envelope with a single exclusive rename, seals what it published read-only, writes control documents, generation documents, and release tags durably, and lets the operator-only maintenance tooling inspect a root without following links. Its policy lives above it: the core's ingest, revision, release, and collection services decide what to write and when; core.rawstore decides how a write becomes durable and visible.

    This is one class model presented in focused views. It includes every class declared in src/huron/core/rawstore/ together with the module-level functions those classes are composed from, the consumer-owned RawStore port in core/raw/ports.py, Catalog's narrow GenerationStorage, and Integrity's LegacyStorage/EvidenceStorage ports that the two concrete stores satisfy, plus Catalog/Raw path types and domain services at their points of collaboration. Repeated boxes denote the same class. Core service internals, PostgreSQL adapters, and the catalog's document models are outside this atlas; the catalog atlas covers them. Module boxes list functions with their principal parameters; long parameter lists are abbreviated. This is a Python structure diagram, not a filesystem layout specification or an exhaustive signature reference.

    Currency matters: the inspected package contains no sweeper, retention worker, reconciler, purge, or trash mechanism. The Raw layer design describes those as planned, and the package does not delete anything except its own upload inputs, unpublished candidates, and temporary files. minihuron/rawstore.py and minihuron/rawdatastore.py are a standalone prototype that nothing under src/ imports; they are excluded here. Rawstore is a Core adapter owner; its only Huron dependency is schema.storage. It satisfies consumer ports structurally without importing domains. This atlas describes the verified migration; its evidence is recorded in the roadmap.

    Reading the diagrams

    • A --> B: association/reference, including a held instance or a bound root.
    • A ..> B: uses, creates, or returns B; the label states which.
    • A *-- B: A contains B as part of its object structure.
    • A --|> B: actual Python inheritance.
    • A ..|> B: structural conformance to a Python protocol, not inheritance.
    • <<Protocol>>, <<Module>>, <<Frozen>>, <<NamedTuple>>, <<External>>, and <<Neighbor>> identify roles. A <<Module>> box lists a module's public functions; private helpers appear only where they explain structure.
    • Descriptor parameters are integers: every traversal below a held directory uses dir_fd opens with O_NOFOLLOW, never a path string, so a symbolic link planted in the tree is refused rather than followed.
    • Durability claims describe what the code does before returning: every primitive fsyncs the bytes it wrote and then the directory that names them.

    1. The rawstore at a glance

    The overview separates the two concrete stores by consumer. PosixRawStore is the production RawStore that the API runtime constructs once and every core service writes through. MaintenanceStore is constructed by the lakectl wiring and controller for the operator-only integrity subsystem and never by the API. Both are built from the same descriptor-holding primitives in materialize.

    Responsibility Owner Important contract
    Claim a private session root PosixRawStore.create_staging Direct child of root/.staging; upload, completion, and envelope/payload created at 0o700; a second claim on the same name fails at mkdir.
    Receive upload parts PosixRawStore.write_part Positional writes into [offset, offset + length) of an input that may already exist; exact length enforced; file and ancestors flushed before success; the ledger records that durable progress.
    Materialize verified files PosixRawStore.finish_file with CompletionAdmission A bounded, capacity-reserved copy into a closed 0o444 candidate, installed by exclusive rename; a mismatch installs nothing; a concurrent winner is verified, not replaced.
    Publish a revision commit.commit_envelope Requires COMMITTED; flushes the tree; one exclusive rename; never overwrites an existing final; a completed commit may be retried.
    Seal published bytes PosixRawStore.seal / flush_tree Files 0o444, descendant directories 0o555, root untouched so it can still be renamed.
    Write control documents write_document, write_tag_once, write_generation, atomic_replace Documents and tags are write-once; generation files and CURRENT.json are replaced atomically because immutability is guaranteed above this layer.
    Verify evidence inspection.verify_envelope Exact inventory, independent owned inodes, frozen document bytes; optional sealed check on descendants only.
    Inspect and record for maintenance MaintenanceStore No-follow enumeration, bounded control reads, streamed inspection with finding codes, write-once protocol evidence, and a flock claim.

    2. The RawStore port and its POSIX implementation

    Sources: Raw ports, Catalog generation port, store.py, init.py, app.py.

    The ports are declared by their consumers, Raw and Catalog, and Rawstore never imports them; conformance is structural, and the store's own docstring names the protocol it satisfies. Two shape differences are worth knowing. The protocol declares root as a read-only property while the store exposes a plain public attribute, and the store's atomic_replace accepts an extra keyword mode that the protocol does not declare; both remain compatible with every current caller.

    The application lifespan constructs one PosixRawStore from ApiSettings, calls initialize() so a cross-device layout fails at startup, and publishes it in ApiRuntime. Raw workflows receive it typed as RawStore; Catalog receives GenerationStorage. Catalog's asynchronous GenerationDocuments.write() owns off-thread serialization and storage. Other blocking workflow calls run through asyncify, because the store is synchronous and blocking. Clock is a Foundation port. The application-owned combined Storage capability verifies that one POSIX object satisfies both consumer interfaces at wiring time.

    3. Staging, part receipt, and verified completion

    Sources: store.py, completion.py, materialize.py, storage.py, Raw staging paths.

    Session root. create_staging accepts only a direct child of root/.staging and creates the session directory with a plain mkdir that must succeed, so the name itself is the ingest's claim. upload, completion, and envelope/payload are created beneath it at 0o700 and each is fsynced before the call returns.

    Parts. write_part validates rel_path through _safe_relative (no absolute paths, no empty, ., or .. components; a leading payload/ is tolerated but must not be the whole path), opens the input with O_CREAT but without truncation, refuses anything that is not a regular, singly linked file owned by the current user, and streams exactly length bytes with positional writes. Nothing is buffered beyond one chunk; each chunk is on disk before the next is pulled. A stream that runs short or long raises PartLengthMismatchError, which schema/storage.py owns and the package re-exports.

    Completion. finish_file first tries _installed_payload: if the target already exists under envelope/payload it must observe the declared size and digest, otherwise the call fails. Only when the target is missing does _copy_file take a CompletionAdmission slot, re-check for a concurrent winner, reserve the expected byte count against statvfs free space (raising ENOSPC when the configured reserve cannot be retained), copy the upload input through file_chunks into a closed 0o444 candidate, observe it, and install it by exclusive rename only when the observation matches. A mismatch returns the observed pair and installs nothing; the caller decides what that means. Reservations are per store instance and per process; other processes and held upload descriptors are not fenced.

    Discard. discard_file unlinks an upload input and fsyncs its directory; a missing input is success.

    4. Commit publication

    Sources: commit.py, materialize.py, private Raw ingestion.

    commit_envelope refuses a path that escapes the trusted root, then holds descriptors for both parents and calls _publish. The decision table inside _publish is the whole publication protocol:

    Final exists Staging exists COMMITTED present Outcome
    no yes no ValueError; nothing published
    no yes yes flush tree, exclusive rename, fsync both parents, fchmod 0o555 and fsync final
    yes yes any FileExistsError; an existing revision is never replaced
    yes no in final retry path: fsync both parents and reseal final
    yes no absent from final FileNotFoundError from the marker check

    The rename is renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE) on Linux and renameatx_np on macOS, loaded through ctypes; any other platform, or a C library without the call, raises ENOTSUP. A device mismatch is detected twice: at startup by assert_same_filesystem, which creates both roots and compares st_dev, and again immediately before the rename. Both report CrossDeviceCommitError carrying errno.EXDEV.

    Ordering in the ingest workflow. IngestService writes the frozen intent documents into the envelope, verifies the staged envelope against the manifest and documents, seals it, and commits it. If any step fails with OSError or ValueError it verifies the final path with sealed=True instead, which is how a crash or a concurrent committer is distinguished from corruption. It then verifies the final path again and calls commit_envelope once more so the retry branch reseals and flushes. The store does not check evidence on the retry branch itself; the caller must have verified first, and the ingest workflow does. Descriptor-based materialize.flush_tree owns child-before-parent durability and sealed-tree checks. commit.fsync_dir remains the single-directory primitive.

    5. Control documents, generations, tags, and the revision index

    Sources: store.py, Catalog generation documents, Raw releases, private Raw ingestion.

    Four write disciplines coexist, chosen by what the record means:

    • Envelope documents (write_document): the name must be a single component and not one of "", ., .., or payload. The bytes become a closed candidate in the session's completion directory and are installed at the envelope root by exclusive rename; equal existing bytes are a retry, different bytes fail. A missing session root is never recreated.
    • Release tags (write_tag_once through _write_once): O_EXCL create at 0o444, whole payload, fsync file, fsync directory. Retagging fails with FileExistsError. _write_once has no other caller.
    • Generation documents and CURRENT.json (write_generation through atomic_replace): the numbered file is replaced atomically, then the pointer is replaced atomically. Immutability of an acknowledged generation is enforced by the hierarchy store's version-guarded commit, not by the filesystem; a file already present at that number can only be an unacknowledged crashed attempt. The two replacements are ordered, not joint. The generation number must lie in 1..999_999.
    • INDEX.json (atomic_replace from the ingest workflow): best effort after a successful commit; a failure is logged and never fails the commit, because the index is derivable from the revision directories.

    atomic_replace writes to a .{name}.XXXXXX temporary beside the target, sets the mode, fsyncs, closes, os.replaces, then fsyncs the directory; on any earlier failure the temporary is removed and the target is untouched. It is the one primitive in the package that overwrites, and it uses path strings rather than held descriptors.

    6. Inspection and revision reads

    Sources: inspection.py, store.py, private Raw reader, private Raw ingestion.

    verify_envelope builds one expected inventory from the manifest entries and the frozen control documents, derives the set of directories that inventory implies (always including payload), and walks the envelope with held descriptors. At every level the directory listing must equal the expected names exactly; every regular file must observe its declared size and digest through a read-only, no-follow descriptor on a singly linked inode owned by the current user; every directory must be owned by the current user. With sealed=True files must be read-only and descendant directories 0o555; the envelope root is never required to be sealed because publication renames it before commit_envelope seals it. Any disagreement is a ValueError naming the offending path but not its content.

    read_document and stat_document are direct path operations with no traversal discipline; they serve committed control documents and payload files whose locations the core services derive from committed manifests and revision records. The revision reader re-resolves permission and stats the payload before streaming it; that policy is the core's, not the store's.

    7. Descriptor discipline shared by both stores

    Source: materialize.py.

    Every function takes or yields file descriptors. directory opens a path with O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW; when given an anchor it instead opens the anchor and walks each relative component through descendant, refusing ... descendant duplicates the parent descriptor and steps one component at a time, optionally creating missing directories privately at 0o700 and fsyncing the parent after each mkdir. candidate allocates a uuid4-named file with O_EXCL, writes all chunks, seals it 0o444, fsyncs and closes it, fsyncs the parent, yields the name, and unlinks whatever remains on exit. install renames the candidate exclusively; on FileExistsError it verifies the existing target against the expected pair and accepts a matching winner. write_all loops over short writes and raises EIO on zero progress. flush_tree refuses any non-regular or shared file, optionally seals as it goes, and fsyncs each directory after its children; the root's mode is left alone.

    8. Maintenance inspection and the integrity port

    Sources: maintenance.py, integrity/ports.py, Integrity controller implementation, lakectl/wiring.py, lakectl/controller.py.

    MaintenanceStore is bound to a root and a deployment-assigned owner UID; it is constructed by lakectl wiring and injected into Integrity's cutover and controller-admission operations. It never interprets catalog documents and never publishes revisions. LegacyStorage is runtime_checkable, and the store satisfies it structurally. ControllerAdmission owns epoch, receipt-admission and restart-exclusion policy; the application owns Podman, peer authentication, durable state I/O and serialization. CutoverService owns stored-sequence reading/validation; the full legacy scan stays outside the serialized controller request loop. Activation and general recovery remain planned.

    • Enumeration walks organization/*/project/*/dataset/*/raw/revision/* for revisions and each entity's CURRENT.json plus generations/* for control documents, always through held descriptors and in sorted order. A missing generations directory or pointer surfaces as an error rather than a skipped entity.
    • Bounded reads refuse non-regular files and anything above 64 MiB. read_generation additionally requires the configured owner, a sealed mode, and a single link; read_control checks size and kind only, so a corrupt document keeps its original bytes for the caller to judge.
    • Inspection hashes every regular file, records directories as inventory entries, and accumulates finding codes: WRONG_OWNER, UNSEALED, SHARED_INODE, UNSAFE_ENTRY, ENTRY_IO_ERROR, and INVENTORY_MISMATCH when an expected inventory is supplied. Corrupt siblings do not stop the walk.
    • Evidence is installed under protocol/ through a candidate in protocol/workspace and an exclusive rename; conflicting existing bytes fail.
    • Claim takes flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB) on protocol/.maintenance.lock, refusing a lock inode that is not private, singly linked, and owned by the caller. The lock is released by descriptor close or process death, never by a timer, and the inode is never unlinked.

    9. Errors, layout types, and what is not here

    Sources: commit.py, storage.py, Raw paths, Catalog paths, Foundation names.

    The package declares exactly one exception, CrossDeviceCommitError, and re-exports PartLengthMismatchError from schema/storage.py. Everything else it raises is a builtin: ValueError for unsafe names, missing COMMITTED, conflicting installed content, and inventory disagreement; FileExistsError for a second tag or an occupied final path; FileNotFoundError for missing documents and session roots; OSError with ENOSPC, EIO, or ENOTSUP for capacity, stalled writes, and unsupported exclusive rename. No rawstore error carries an HTTP status; the core translates storage failures into catalog domain errors.

    The store receives domain layout paths: core.raw.paths builds staging, revision and tag locations, core.catalog.paths builds hierarchy/generation/cross-layer locations, and Foundation owns lexical validation. parse_revision_dir is the inverse used when a stored revision_path must be interpreted.

    Declared in design, absent in code: TTL expiration, holds, purge, the staging-trash sweeper, the nightly reconciler with budgeted hashing, and automatic INDEX/CURRENT repair from the Raw layer design have no implementation in core.rawstore. The closest existing capabilities are MaintenanceStore.inspect_revision, which only reports, and the ingest workflow's lapsed-session expiry, which lives in the core and the metastore rather than in this package.

    Source and behavioral cross-checks

    The implementation snapshot was traced through constructors, fields, protocol declarations, module imports, and call sites in the core, API, and lakectl applications. Useful behavioral entry points for our next discussion are:

    • Store tests, materialize tests, and completion admission tests: staging claims, part ranges, safe paths, candidates, exclusive install, slots and capacity reservation.
    • Commit tests and commit intent contracts: the publication decision table, cross-device refusal, and retry behavior.
    • Generation tests and inspection tests: generation and pointer replacement, envelope inventory and seal verification.
    • Process-death contracts and ingest crash matrix: what survives a crash between the store's ordered steps.
    • Maintenance ownership contracts, integrity storage tests, and legacy verification tests: the MaintenanceStore claim, finding codes, and evidence writes.

    This document describes inspected implementation; it does not claim that the application test suites were rerun to create a diagram.
